plan.angle: Keep the decoder exactly as planned, with these locks: hook 'Did retatrutide beat tirzepatide? No trial has compared them. In a 48-week Phase 2 trial, the top dose averaged 24.2%.' TRIUMPH-2 uses the Lancet figures only (12.7% / 19.1% / 20.8% vs 4.0% placebo at 80 weeks, 1,152 adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity or overweight), with the estimand named and A1C taken from the paper. TRIUMPH-3 is 'Lilly reported up to 22.6% at 80 weeks in adults with severe obesity and established cardiovascular disease'. Status: 'Not approved by the FDA, MHRA, Health Canada or TGA as of Oct 2026. Lilly says it plans to submit to the FDA in Q1 2027.' Keep the FDA warning about online products, the per-arm side effects, the 'don't switch or stop' line and the prescriber line.
plan.working_title: Did Retatrutide Beat Tirzepatide? How the Triple-Hormone Shot Works (24.2%, Phase 2)
plan.why: Decoders of next-gen drugs are our only long-form lane that travels (median ~32, EloraTZP 396). Lilly's Q3 earnings around Oct 29 and the bootleg news are driving demand, and the body rests on peer-reviewed NEJM and Lancet papers. | fact-check: Topic and structure are sound and fit the strongest long-form lane (next-gen decoder, 'Did X beat tirzepatide?'). Checked: Phase 2 top dose 24.2% at 48 weeks (NEJM 2023). TRIUMPH-2: 1,152 adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity or overweight, 4/9/12 mg for 80 weeks. Weight loss was 12.7%, 19.1% and 20.8% vs 4.0% on placebo, published in The Lancet and presented at EASD 2026 (epocrates). Lilly's 23 Jul 2026 topline gave the same 20.8% vs 3.2% placebo and an A1C fall of up to 1.6%, against about 1.4–1.5% in the paper. The two figures most likely use different estimands, so they will conflict unless labelled. TRIUMPH-3 per Lilly: up to 22.6% at 80 weeks in adults with severe obesity and established cardiovascular disease. Lilly plans a BLA submission to the FDA in Q1 2027 (Lilly press release, HCPLive 23 Jul 2026). Problems to fix: (a) use only the Lancet placebo figure (4.0%) and its A1C figure, name the estimand, and don't mix in the topline 3.2% or 1.6%; (b) the hook number 24.2% comes from a 48-week Phase 2 trial in people without diabetes, so the first line has to say 'Phase 2, 48 weeks' and answer 'no head-to-head' right away; (c) TRIUMPH-3 population is 'severe obesity with established cardiovascular disease', credited as 'Lilly reported'; (d) write the filing plan as 'Lilly says it plans to submit to the FDA in Q1 2027'. That's a plan, not a filing or an approval.

package.description:
Did retatrutide beat tirzepatide? We don't know yet: no trial has compared them head to head. In a 48-week Phase 2 trial (NEJM, 2023) in adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes, retatrutide's top dose averaged 24.2% weight loss vs 2.1% on placebo, assuming people stayed on treatment. Nausea and other digestive side effects were most common. As of October 2026, retatrutide is not approved by the FDA, MHRA, Health Canada or TGA.

This video is education, not medical advice. Don't switch, stop or change your current medicines on your own. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

Sources:
Jastreboff AM et al., NEJM 2023: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2301972
TRIUMPH-2, The Lancet (online 29 Sep 2026): https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(26)01861-1/abstract
Eli Lilly news release, 23 Jul 2026: https://investor.lilly.com/news-releases/news-release-details/lillys-triple-agonist-retatrutide-successful-two-additional

script.working_title: Did Retatrutide Beat Tirzepatide? How the Triple-Hormone Shot Works (24.2%, Phase 2)
script.hook_pattern: Open loop: the first line answers the title question (no head-to-head trial yet) and gives the Phase 2 number (24.2% at 48 weeks). A second loop opens straight after, the glucagon blood-sugar puzzle, and it pays off in the Phase 3 TRIUMPH chapter.

scenes.narration: Did retatrutide beat tirzepatide? No trial has compared them head to head. But in a 48-week Phase 2 trial, the top dose averaged 24.2% weight loss.

visual.stock_query: two cartoon syringes facing off, question mark

scenes.retention_device: Title question answered in line one, with a specific number that creates curiosity

scenes.narration: That trial was in adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes. And that 24.2% is exactly why your feed is full of this drug.

visual.stock_query: big glowing number above curious crowd

scenes.retention_device: Specific proof point, with its population, placed right after the hook

scenes.narration: Maybe you've seen it. A late-night scroll, a Reddit thread, someone calling it the next big thing. And a small voice asks: should I be on that instead?

visual.stock_query: person scrolling phone in bed, worried

scenes.retention_device: Lived moment the viewer recognises

scenes.narration: If that's you, the question is completely normal. Wanting the best option for your health isn't greedy or impatient. Anyone would wonder.

visual.stock_query: Medi mascot giving reassuring thumbs up

scenes.retention_device: Names the feeling and validates it

scenes.narration: So here's what you'll get: how a three-hormone shot works, what its trials actually found, how they stack up against tirzepatide's, and where it stands as of October 2026.
scenes.retention_device: Clear promise of what the viewer will get

scenes.narration: And keep one puzzle in mind. The third hormone this drug targets, glucagon, normally pushes blood sugar up. So why add it to a drug that's also being tested in people with type 2 diabetes? The answer comes later.
scenes.retention_device: Open loop that pays off in the TRIUMPH-2 chapter

scenes.narration: Let's follow one person. Imagine Dana, 48. She's been on tirzepatide for a year, with her prescriber, and retatrutide headlines keep landing in her feed.

visual.stock_query: woman at kitchen table reading phone, curious

scenes.retention_device: Introduces the hypothetical thread character

scenes.narration: First, the biology. Every time you eat, your gut releases hormones that send messages to your brain, your pancreas and your liver.

visual.stock_query: gut sending glowing messages to brain

scenes.retention_device: Chapter change into the mechanism

scenes.narration: One of them is GLP-1. It helps release insulin when blood sugar is high, slows how fast your stomach empties, and helps signal fullness to your brain.

visual.stock_query: cartoon pancreas, stomach and brain team

scenes.retention_device: Simple three-part explanation

scenes.narration: Semaglutide, the medicine in Ozempic and Wegovy, acts on that GLP-1 receptor. Tirzepatide, sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound, adds a second target: GIP, another gut hormone involved in insulin release.

visual.stock_query: one key and two keys unlocking doors

scenes.retention_device: Builds step by step toward the third target

scenes.narration: Retatrutide adds a third: the glucagon receptor. It's one weekly injection with three hormone targets, which is why it's called a triple agonist.

visual.stock_query: three keys on one keyring glowing

scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the build-up, with the key term defined

scenes.narration: Think of a sound desk. Semaglutide moves one slider, tirzepatide two, retatrutide three. More sliders doesn't automatically mean better music. It just gives more ways to tune it.

visual.stock_query: cartoon sound mixing desk with three sliders

scenes.retention_device: Vivid analogy that makes the idea stick

scenes.narration: So what does glucagon add? In mouse studies, the glucagon part appeared to raise energy expenditure, meaning the body used more energy. That's an animal finding, not proof it works the same way in people.
scenes.on_screen_text: Mouse finding, not proof in people

visual.stock_query: lab mouse on tiny treadmill, smiling

scenes.retention_device: Surprising mechanism, hedged honestly

scenes.narration: Researchers are also interested in glucagon's effects on fat in the liver. Hold that thought, because one of the most striking results in this video is about the liver.
scenes.retention_device: New open loop, paid off in 'Beyond the scale'

scenes.narration: Now, the trial that started the buzz. It was published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2023.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter change: the micro-story of the trial

scenes.narration: 338 adults took part. All had obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, and none had diabetes. They got weekly retatrutide at one of several doses, or placebo, for 48 weeks.

visual.stock_query: diverse group of cartoon volunteers waving

scenes.retention_device: Concrete trial design

scenes.narration: Results climbed with the dose. At 48 weeks, average weight loss was 8.7% on the lowest dose, then 17.1% and 22.8% on the two middle dose levels.
scenes.retention_device: Escalating numbers build toward the headline figure

scenes.narration: And on the highest dose: 24.2% among 62 people, compared with 2.1% among 70 people on placebo.
scenes.retention_device: Pays off the hook number, with group sizes

scenes.narration: To picture it: for someone starting at 100 kilos, or 220 pounds, 24.2% is about 24 kilos, or 53 pounds, in under a year. But that's an average. People varied.

visual.stock_query: bag of sugar stack on balance scale

scenes.retention_device: Puts the number in everyday terms

scenes.narration: Another way to see it: on the highest dose, 83% lost at least 15% of their body weight by week 48, compared with 2% on placebo.

visual.stock_query: pie chart with happy cartoon people

scenes.retention_device: Second surprising stat that keeps momentum

scenes.narration: And here's what made headlines. On the higher doses, weight hadn't levelled off by week 48, so we don't know where it would have settled.

visual.stock_query: line graph still sloping, question mark

scenes.retention_device: Mini-cliffhanger: we don't know where it ends

scenes.narration: But pause. 338 people over 48 weeks is a Phase 2 trial. It's built to choose doses and spot safety signals, not to settle how one drug compares with another.
scenes.retention_device: 'But' turn that leads into the comparison chapter

scenes.narration: So how does tirzepatide's evidence look? Its big obesity trial, SURMOUNT-1, was published in 2022 in the same journal.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter change: the other side of the matchup

scenes.narration: It enrolled adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes. Treatment lasted 72 weeks, about half a year longer than the retatrutide trial.
scenes.retention_device: Plants the timeline difference used later

scenes.narration: Counting everyone randomised, whether or not they stayed on the drug, average weight loss was 15.0%, 19.5% and 20.9% across the three tirzepatide doses, versus 3.1% on placebo.
scenes.retention_device: Names the analysis, which sets up the dropout point later

scenes.narration: The highest-dose group had 630 people, and placebo had 643. The whole trial had 2,539 people, more than seven times as many as retatrutide's Phase 2.

visual.stock_query: huge crowd next to small crowd

scenes.retention_device: Turns trial size into a picture

scenes.narration: Tirzepatide also has something retatrutide doesn't yet: a published head-to-head. In SURMOUNT-5, adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes, were followed for 72 weeks.
scenes.retention_device: Contrast: what a fair comparison looks like

scenes.narration: At their highest tolerated doses, tirzepatide averaged 20.2% weight loss among 374 people, versus 13.7% on semaglutide among 377.
scenes.retention_device: Concrete head-to-head number

scenes.narration: That kind of trial really can answer 'which did better?' Same trial, same rules, same timeline. Retatrutide hasn't had one yet.
scenes.retention_device: Shows what's missing for retatrutide

scenes.narration: Back to Dana. She sees 24.2% next to 20.9% and it's tempting to call it. But here's where it gets tricky.
scenes.retention_device: Thread callback plus 'here's where it gets tricky' cliffhanger

scenes.section: Why you can't line them up
scenes.narration: Comparing numbers from separate trials is like comparing marathon times from different courses, with different weather and different runners.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter change opened with an analogy

scenes.section: Why you can't line them up
scenes.narration: Difference one: time. Retatrutide's figure is at 48 weeks, tirzepatide's at 72. A longer trial gives more time to lose weight, and more time for people to drop out.
scenes.retention_device: Numbered countdown structure

scenes.section: Why you can't line them up
scenes.narration: Difference two: size. With 62 people in a dose group, an average can swing much more than with 630.

visual.stock_query: small seesaw tipping, large one steady

scenes.retention_device: Short, punchy contrast

scenes.section: Why you can't line them up
scenes.narration: Difference three: how dropouts are counted. Some analyses include everyone randomised. Others estimate what happens if people stay on treatment. Those choices move the numbers. Retatrutide's 24.2% assumes people stayed on treatment. Tirzepatide's 20.9% counts everyone randomised. Measured the stay-on-treatment way, tirzepatide's top dose averaged 22.5%.
scenes.retention_device: Insider detail most viewers haven't heard, which reframes the 24.2% vs 20.9% comparison

scenes.section: Why you can't line them up
scenes.narration: Difference four: the people themselves. Starting weight, age and where the trial ran all shape the averages.
scenes.retention_device: Closes the countdown

scenes.section: Why you can't line them up
scenes.narration: So the honest scorecard: retatrutide's Phase 2 number is impressive, but it doesn't prove it beats tirzepatide. Not proven isn't the same as disproven, either.

visual.fact: Different trials, timelines and analyses. No head-to-head yet

scenes.retention_device: Myth/fact payoff of the comparison section

scenes.section: Why you can't line them up
scenes.narration: Is there any better evidence? Yes, sort of. Retatrutide's larger Phase 3 trials, called TRIUMPH, have started reporting. And one of them solves our glucagon puzzle.
scenes.retention_device: Re-hook that brings back the glucagon open loop

scenes.narration: TRIUMPH-2 was published in The Lancet. It enrolled 1,152 adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity or overweight, randomised to one of three retatrutide doses or placebo for 80 weeks.

visual.stock_query: large trial crowd with glucose meters

scenes.retention_device: Chapter change to bigger, newer evidence

scenes.narration: Counting everyone randomised, whether or not they stayed on the drug, average weight loss at 80 weeks was 11.9%, 16.8% and 18.8% across the three doses, versus 5.1% on placebo. If everyone had stayed on treatment, the estimate was 12.7%, 19.1% and 20.8%, versus 4.0%.
scenes.retention_device: Fresh Phase 3 numbers, with both analyses named

scenes.narration: Why two sets of numbers? Lilly's headline used the stay-on-treatment estimate. The paper also counts everyone randomised. That's why figures you see online may not match.
scenes.on_screen_text: Two analyses, two sets of numbers
scenes.retention_device: Trust-builder that heads off confusion

scenes.narration: Now the glucagon puzzle. Glucagon normally raises blood sugar. Yet in TRIUMPH-2, A1C, your roughly three-month blood sugar average, fell by 1.4 to 1.6 percentage points on retatrutide, versus 0.2 on placebo, assuming people stayed on treatment.

visual.stock_query: blood sugar meter with downward arrow

scenes.retention_device: Pays off the glucagon open loop from the opening

scenes.narration: How? The molecule was designed to balance glucagon with GLP-1 and GIP, which both help release insulin. In these results, blood sugar still improved overall.
scenes.retention_device: Explains the payoff and moves the story on

scenes.narration: For context, tirzepatide's trial in adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity or overweight, SURMOUNT-2, counting everyone randomised, found 14.7% weight loss on the highest dose among 311 people, versus 3.2% among 315 on placebo, at 72 weeks.
scenes.retention_device: Closest comparison available, which invites the viewer to judge

scenes.narration: That's 18.8% for retatrutide's top dose at 80 weeks, and 14.7% for tirzepatide's at 72. But these are separate trials with different timelines. It hints. It doesn't decide.

visual.stock_query: two puzzle pieces not quite fitting

scenes.retention_device: 'But' beat that keeps the viewer honest

scenes.narration: Then there's TRIUMPH-3. In 1,949 adults with severe obesity and established cardiovascular disease, Lilly reported 22.6% weight loss on the top dose at 80 weeks, versus 3.2% on placebo, assuming people stayed on treatment.
scenes.retention_device: New stat for a new population

scenes.narration: That's a company-reported figure. The full peer-reviewed paper, with every analysis and side effect, is what to look for.

visual.stock_query: Medi reading press release, eyebrow raised

scenes.retention_device: Teaches viewers to tell a paper from a press release

scenes.narration: So did retatrutide beat tirzepatide in either trial? Neither one included tirzepatide. The honest answer hasn't changed.
scenes.retention_device: Main loop restated before the next chapter

scenes.narration: Remember the liver? Here's the result I promised.
scenes.retention_device: Pays off the liver open loop

scenes.narration: In a Phase 2 substudy published in Nature Medicine in 2024, researchers measured liver fat in people from the obesity trial who started with at least 10% fat in their liver.
scenes.retention_device: Micro-story of the study design

scenes.narration: After 24 weeks, liver fat fell by an average of 81.4% and 82.4% on the two highest doses. On placebo, it rose slightly, by 0.3%.

visual.stat_label: Relative liver fat drop, top dose, 24 weeks

scenes.retention_device: The most striking stat, held back until late

scenes.narration: That's a relative drop. Picture a liver that's 20% fat falling to under 4%.
scenes.retention_device: Puts the percentage into a picture

scenes.narration: But it's a small, early study, and less liver fat isn't proof of fewer liver problems later. It's why researchers are watching this drug for fatty liver disease.
scenes.retention_device: Honest hedge that leads into the next chapter

scenes.narration: Now the part every honest decoder needs: side effects.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter change; the viewer expects balance

scenes.narration: In retatrutide's Phase 2 trial, the most common side effects were gastrointestinal, such as nausea. They rose with dose and were mostly mild to moderate.
scenes.retention_device: Plain-language safety detail

scenes.narration: Starting at a lower dose partly eased them. Heart rate also rose with dose, peaking at 24 weeks and easing after that.
scenes.retention_device: Adds a lesser-known detail

scenes.narration: In the larger TRIUMPH-2 trial, nausea affected 13.7%, 20.8% and 28.0% across the three doses, versus 8.0% on placebo. Diarrhoea was the most common side effect.

visual.stock_query: four bars with gentle stomach icons

scenes.retention_device: Phase 3 per-arm safety numbers that balance the Phase 3 benefits

scenes.narration: Tirzepatide's SURMOUNT-1 trial gave per-dose figures. Nausea affected 24.6%, 33.3% and 31.0% across the three doses, versus 9.5% on placebo.
scenes.retention_device: Per-arm numbers keep the comparison honest

scenes.narration: And 4.3%, 7.1% and 6.2% stopped tirzepatide because of side effects, versus 2.6% on placebo.

visual.stock_query: small group stepping off a path

scenes.retention_device: Concrete number on tolerability

scenes.narration: In that trial, digestive side effects happened mainly while doses were being increased. That's why dose changes are a prescriber's call, never a solo experiment.
scenes.retention_device: Turns data into a safety takeaway

scenes.narration: If you're dealing with nausea on any GLP-1 medicine right now, you're not doing anything wrong. Tell your prescriber. There are often practical ways to make it easier.

visual.stock_query: Medi offering comforting cup of tea

scenes.retention_device: Validates the viewer and gives agency

scenes.narration: So where does retatrutide stand today?
scenes.retention_device: Chapter change with a direct question

scenes.narration: As of October 2026, retatrutide is an investigational medicine. Lilly has not yet filed it with the FDA, and it isn't approved by the FDA, the UK's MHRA, Health Canada or Australia's TGA.
scenes.on_screen_text: Not approved: FDA, MHRA, Health Canada, TGA (Oct 2026)
scenes.retention_device: Dated status line

scenes.narration: Lilly says it plans to submit to the FDA in the first quarter of 2027. That's a plan. It isn't a filing, and it isn't an approval.

visual.myth: Retatrutide is about to be approved
visual.fact: Lilly plans to submit to the FDA in Q1 2027. Not approved

scenes.retention_device: Corrects the common assumption; a new loop to follow

scenes.narration: Tirzepatide, by contrast, is FDA-approved: as Mounjaro for type 2 diabetes, and since November 2023 as Zepbound for chronic weight management.
scenes.retention_device: Contrast that grounds the viewer

scenes.narration: Here's the safety part. The FDA has warned about unapproved GLP-1 drugs sold online, which haven't been reviewed by the FDA for safety, quality or effectiveness.

visual.stock_query: warning sign over laptop shopping cart

scenes.retention_device: Protective information at a natural turning point

scenes.narration: So anything sold online as retatrutide today is not an approved medicine, and there's no way to know it matches what was studied. Please don't go looking for it.

visual.stock_query: mystery vial with question mark label

scenes.retention_device: Direct, caring safety message

scenes.narration: If you're curious about retatrutide, the safest route is a conversation with a prescriber, who can also tell you whether a clinical trial might be an option.
scenes.retention_device: Gives a safe next step

scenes.narration: So, back to the question we started with: did retatrutide beat tirzepatide?
scenes.retention_device: Returns to the main loop before the payoff

scenes.narration: Answer: we don't know yet. No trial has compared them head to head. Retatrutide's numbers are impressive, but they come from different trials, people and timelines.
scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the main open loop

scenes.narration: And Dana? Her best move isn't chasing a headline. It's bringing her questions to her prescriber, and not switching, stopping or changing her current medicines on her own.
scenes.on_screen_text: Don't switch or stop on your own

visual.stock_query: woman talking calmly with her doctor

scenes.retention_device: Resolves the character thread with agency

scenes.narration: Your checklist for the next headline: Phase 2 or Phase 3? How many weeks? Who was studied? And is it a published paper or a press release?
scenes.retention_device: Practical, reusable takeaway

scenes.narration: One more: ask your prescriber what your current treatment is doing for your health beyond the scale, like blood sugar, blood pressure and how you feel day to day.
scenes.retention_device: Turns the focus to the viewer's own health

scenes.narration: And if you're on tirzepatide or semaglutide now, a new drug in the pipeline doesn't make your progress any less real.
scenes.retention_device: Ends the emotional arc on empowerment

scenes.narration: This video is education, not medical advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you, and don't switch, stop or change your current medicines on your own.

factcheck.summary: Claims checked against sources: retatrutide Phase 2 (338 adults, 48 wk, 8.7/17.1/22.8/24.2% vs 2.1%, 83% vs 2% losing ≥15%, weight not levelled off), TRIUMPH-2 (n=1,152, 80 wk; counting everyone 11.9/16.8/18.8 vs 5.1; if everyone stayed on treatment 12.7/19.1/20.8 vs 4.0; A1C −1.4/−1.6/−1.5 vs −0.2 on the stay-on-treatment figures; nausea 13.7/20.8/28.0 vs 8.0; diarrhoea most common at 27.4–33.6%), TRIUMPH-3 as Lilly reported it (n=1,949, BMI ≥35 plus heart or blood-vessel disease, 22.6% vs 3.2%), and the status (Lilly calls it 'investigational', plans FDA submission Q1 2027). The Phase 2 paper itself is paywalled; searches confirmed 24.2% and the design, and the other Phase 2 figures plus which analysis method gave 24.2% match prior knowledge of the paper. SURMOUNT-1/-2/-5, the liver substudy and the mechanism papers match prior knowledge but were not re-opened. Framing is sound: no head-to-head is stated plainly, analysis methods are named, the timeline gap is shown, the mouse finding is hedged, company figures are attributed, Dana is labelled hypothetical, the status is dated for 4 regulators, and the gray-market, prescriber and don't-switch lines are present. Three minor polish items only.

thumbnail.reasoning: All three are legible at phone size, but #0's scorecard-style red X / green check marks declare retatrutide the clear winner over tirzepatide, directly contradicting its own headline 'NEVER TESTED' and the video's actual nuanced finding — that's a misleading-verdict risk the instructions say to avoid, even though its raw curiosity pull is probably highest. #2 is clean and uses our proven 'approved yet?' curiosity format, but its promised payoff (approval status) doesn't match the title's actual promise (a Phase 2 efficacy number/comparison), creating a bait-and-switch gap. #1 ('3 HORMONES / ONE SHOT') is the safest strong performer: it's the most legible of the three, has a clear single focal point and specific-number hook, and stays truthful to the mechanism story the video actually tells, while still implying retatrutide's edge over tirzepatide without overclaiming a 'winner.'
